questions.question: 1. Which one of the following is an application of a directed graph?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A mobile communication network can be represented using a graph, but this option does not specifically illustrate the dependency relationship represented by a directed graph.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A water network is commonly represented using a graph, but the option does not specifically describe a prerequisite or dependency relationship.
explanations.c: Correct. Course prerequisites have a direction: one course must be completed before another course can be taken, so they can be represented using directed edges.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A friendship relationship is generally mutual, so it is commonly represented using an undirected graph.

questions.question: 2. If $m$ and $n$ represent the number of vertices and edges respectively, which one of the following combinations cannot be true for a graph?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A graph can have one or more vertices and one or more edges.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A graph can contain vertices without containing any edges.
explanations.c: Correct. An edge connects vertices, so a graph cannot contain an edge when there are no vertices.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A graph can contain many vertices while having only a small number of edges.

questions.question: 3. Which data structure can be used to represent a graph using an adjacency matrix and provides random access to its entries?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A linked list does not provide direct random access to its elements.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A tree is a graph structure, but it is not the underlying data structure normally used to provide random access to adjacency-matrix entries.
explanations.c: Correct. An adjacency matrix can be stored as a two-dimensional array, allowing direct access to an entry using its row and column indices.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A graph is the structure being represented; it is not the array-like storage structure that provides random access to matrix entries.

questions.question: 4. When performing DFS on a directed graph, how does the traversal move from a vertex?

answers.a: It can move along any edge regardless of its direction.
answers.b: It always moves to the vertex with the smallest label.
answers.c: It always moves to the vertex with the largest label.
answers.d: It follows the explicitly directed edges from the current vertex.

explanations.a: Incorrect. A DFS traversal of a directed graph must respect the direction of its edges.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS does not require choosing the adjacent vertex with the smallest label.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not require choosing the adjacent vertex with the largest label.
explanations.d: Correct. In a directed graph, DFS follows edges in their specified direction when moving from one vertex to another.

questions.question: 5. Which one of the following is an application of a directed graph?

answers.b: Data broadcasting from parent to child nodes
answers.c: Representing parent-child relationships in a family tree

explanations.a: Incorrect. Course prerequisites can be represented by directed edges, but this option describes only one application.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Directed edges can represent one-way broadcasting from a parent node to child nodes, but this is only one possible application.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Parent-child relationships can be represented using directed edges, but this option alone does not include all the listed applications.
explanations.d: Correct. All three situations can use directed edges to represent a relationship or flow from one vertex to another.

questions.question: 6. What is the main purpose of marking a vertex as visited during DFS?

answers.a: To ensure that the vertex is processed at most once during the traversal.
answers.b: To increase the number of edges in the graph.
answers.c: To change a directed graph into an undirected graph.
answers.d: To guarantee that the vertex has no adjacent vertices.

explanations.a: Correct. Marking a vertex as visited prevents DFS from repeatedly processing the same vertex and helps avoid unnecessary revisits.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Marking a vertex does not modify the number of edges in the graph.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A visited marker records traversal state and does not change the direction of graph edges.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A vertex can have several adjacent vertices even after it has been marked as visited.

questions.question: 7. Which statement best describes the order in which DFS explores a graph?

answers.a: It visits all vertices at the same depth before moving deeper.
answers.b: It explores as far as possible along a path before backtracking to explore another path.
answers.c: It always visits vertices in increasing numerical order.
answers.d: It always visits vertices in decreasing numerical order.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Exploring all vertices at the same depth before going deeper describes breadth-first exploration.
explanations.b: Correct. DFS follows a path as deeply as possible and backtracks when there are no further unvisited vertices along that path.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not require vertices to be processed according to their numerical labels.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFS does not require vertices to be processed in decreasing numerical order.

questions.question: 8. For a graph represented using an adjacency list, what is the time complexity of DFS in terms of $V$, the number of vertices, and $E$, the number of edges?

explanations.a: Incorrect. DFS must also examine the relevant edges, so considering only the number of vertices is insufficient in the general case.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS visits vertices as well as examining edges, so the vertex contribution cannot be omitted.
explanations.c: Incorrect. With an adjacency-list representation, DFS does not generally require examining all possible vertex pairs.
explanations.d: Correct. With an adjacency list, DFS visits each vertex and examines each edge a constant number of times, giving $O(V + E)$ time.

questions.question: 9. Consider a connected undirected graph with $V$ vertices. During a DFS traversal, how many tree edges are required to first reach all vertices?

explanations.a: Correct. Each newly discovered vertex except the starting vertex is reached through one tree edge, so a connected graph with $V$ vertices has $V - 1$ DFS tree edges.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The starting vertex is already present before any DFS tree edge is used, so counting one edge for every vertex is too many.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not require two tree edges for every vertex to construct its DFS tree.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The number of DFS tree edges is determined by the number of vertices reached and is smaller than this value for a connected graph.
